title: Kathina, the fifth time
hookLine: the end of the rains, the gift of cloth
tomorrow: on his last night under the tree, who did he call as his witness?

cards: A sweater someone knit for you by hand is a different thing from one off a rack. The Majjhima Nikaya tells of a gift like that.
Mahapajapati, the woman who raised the Buddha after his mother died, spins and weaves a new cloth herself, brings it to him, and asks him to accept it. He answers: give it to the Sangha, Gotami.
Give it to the community, and you'll honor both me and them. She asks again. Same answer.
And Ananda, his attendant, can't stand by. He steps in to plead her case.

teach.b: Here's Ananda's case, and it's a strong one. Please accept it, he says. She is your mother's sister.
She nursed you and fed you with her own milk when your mother died. Gratitude to one person is real, and a gift made by hand for one face means something a pile of cloth for a crowd can't.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA: GIVE TO THE MANY.
teach.b: The Buddha doesn't deny a word of it. He agrees she helped him greatly, and says he has helped her too. Then he makes the other case.
He lists gifts to individuals, from a Buddha on down, and gifts to the Sangha, the community. And he says a gift to any one person is never more fruitful than a gift to the Sangha.

One way to hear his side: a gift to the community doesn't hang on whether the one monk you love is worthy, or there, or even alive. It keeps the whole thing going. Kathina is built on the Buddha's side.
When the rains retreat ends, lay people bring cloth to the monastery, but they don't pick the monk.
The community decides who receives the robe. And yet Ananda's side never leaves the room. Someone may come to Kathina because of one teacher, one temple, one face they love.

teach.h: LOVE FOR ONE, GIVEN THROUGH MANY.
teach.b: Both views are in the sutta, and Kathina holds them together: love for one person, given through the many.
The rains end in gifts. The debate is about who they're for.

how: In the month after the rains retreat, Theravada lay Buddhists bring robe-cloth and gifts to a monastery where monks kept the retreat; the monks, not the givers, decide together which monk receives the robe.

o: cloth given as the rains end, to the whole community
a gift a lay family gives to its favorite monk
a robe a monk sews alone to mark his ordination

games.q: the cloth and the debate — tap the pairs.

s: at Kathina, the givers pick which monk gets the robe
they bring the cloth; the community decides who receives it.
the Buddha turned the woman who raised him toward the Sangha
he told Mahapajapati to give her cloth to the community, honoring him and them both.
the Buddha said Mahapajapati owed him nothing and brushed off Ananda
he agreed she had helped him greatly before he made the case for the Sangha.

games.q: your aunt says giving to the one monk you love is more real than giving to a crowd. you lean the Buddha's way. what's her best case, from the sutta?
o: Ananda's: she raised him and nursed him; gratitude to one person is real.
a crowd always wastes a gift, so only gifts to one person count.
the Buddha never answered Ananda, so nobody knows his view.
games.why: Ananda argued it for Mahapajapati: she nursed the Buddha when his mother died. the Buddha agreed she'd helped him greatly, and still pointed her to the Sangha.

practice: Find one useful thing in the room that you could give: a warm scarf, a good pen, a phone charger you don't need. Set it by the door now, where it will leave the house with you. Then sit, and let the space it left behind stay empty.

wordCard.voice: Kathina: the robe-cloth offered as the rains end, given to the whole community, which chooses who wears it.

orig.note: Pali: firm; tradition explains it as the frame the robe-cloth was stretched on.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: the rains end in gifts, for the one you love and for the many. Four of seven, given.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 142 (Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta: Mahapajapati's cloth, Ananda's plea, gifts to individuals and to the Sangha)
Vinaya, Mahavagga VII (the kathina: cloth given to the Sangha at the end of the rains, which the community gives to a monk)
